utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the Trial Chamber has been seized with a motion from the Defence for the release of the VWS report. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think events have passed us by with respect to that report. It's been released to us already. Could we withdraw that motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a couple of housekeeping ones. Your Honour, witnesses Cikotic and Jasarevic are coming. They're said to be coming this week. Cikotic is a commander capable of giving evidence concerning certain command -- well, lines of command. He's capable of is shedding some light on certain areas of military doctrine which will be relevant for your consideration when you come to consider part of the case, and it is only part of the case, but when you come to consider that part which concerns command responsibility and the de jure and de facto role of Mr. Halilovic in these events. Jasarevic is a witness of significance too at a high level. He was the head of military security, the -- it's called the SVB. At some point we'll provide some assistance to the Chamber with the acronyms that are used by the different services, but Jasarevic is the head of the military security service and is capable of giving evidence directly about the investigations into both Grabovica and Uzdol and also to give evidence about the lines of command about which you heard some evidence from the witness -- the witness Mr. Gusic but about which will be clearly more evidence. Each of those witnesses therefore is going to give evidence of a somewhat technical nature. In neither case do we have proofing notes. Nor do we have a list of the documents to be tendered through those witnesses. Now, we've already mentioned that the proofing notes have got to come in a timely fashion. With these witnesses, it's not going to be possible to deal with getting their proofing notes the night before. They are not night-before type of witnesses. They are witnesses of significance. If the proofing notes come late, it expands the time of cross-examination. It means that we would be put into the position of having to ask for delays and so on. We don't -- We haven't asked for any delays so far and we want to do that. We want to keep this trial going on. It's going well. And we want to keep that happening. But at the moment we're not being provided with that material. Now, we need it and I ask for it now because there's a -- there's a certainty that the current witness, Witness D, whose name I now have here, will -- he will certainly finish today and the following witness in respect of whom there is likely to be, I'm now told -- I'm told an application for protective measures as well, that witness will not be a lengthy one so we're going to get to Mr. Cikotic tomorrow. That's a certainty. And it's just an unsatisfactory situation from our point of view that we don't have these notes. So I mention it now because we need them. And if we got them by lunchtime today, I would undertake to do everything I can not to -- not to ask for a delay. It may be we don't need a delay because he's otherwise prepared, of course. But it has to happen quickly, and we ask that that be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could I turn to the Prosecution. I believe that the witness told us in his testimony that he had been in The Hague for ten days. If it is true, I believe that the Defence is entitled to have the proofing notes at least a week before his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, in respect to proofing notes, in respect of the witness which is supposed to be coming next, I think those have been provided. In respect of Cikotic, he is being proofed as we speak, Your Honours. And, in fact -- and in respect of Jasarevic, he has not been proofed yet. He just came into The Hague yesterday evening and I'm going to see him today after the court session. Your Honour, perhaps learned counsel does not know the way things are done at this Tribunal, but usually the witnesses are brought just before the -- the evidence and we don't see -- get to see them until two days before, and that's the time we proof them. And the moment we proof them the proofing notes are handed over. And, Your Honours, I would also argue that the proofing notes should not cause any delay to the calling of this witness. All the other statements, all the other material, has been handed over to the Defence and they have ample time to prepare. Proofing notes are just any additional material or any contradictions that the witness has come up with during proofing. So I don't think it's quite fair to say that we are delaying proofing notes because we are not. The moment Cikotic has been proofed, the notes will be provided, and Jasarevic, as I said, has just come in last night, and I haven't even seen him. And in any event, I do not think proofing notes is a good reason to ask for this trial to be delayed to that respect. The proofing notes to date have always been quite short. They have not been particularly significant. And nothing that counsel cannot wrap his mind around at a fairly rapid notice, given that he's got all the other material and knows what these witnesses are going to come to say. And in respect to the documents, Your Honour, it is only after proofing we know the documents which are to be used and we have given -- and given them to the court deputy for them to be entered into e-court and we always hand over the list to the Defence as soon as is practical. We have not delayed in this respect at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: To clarify something that was just said there. Is it being said that the list of documents to be tendered through Jasarevic and Cikotic has been provided to the court deputy? Is that what's being said? Because it hasn't been provided to the Defence here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Will be clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please speak into the microphone. Will the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, please speak to the microphone. You have been reminded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'll be very brief about that. There's just two things, in response. Obviously the documents have to be provided to us quickly and the Prosecution know what they're going to put through this witness. They should have provided that long ago. They should provide it now. Saying that the Defence has had ample time really disguises the fact that the Prosecution has been going for three years here. They must know and they do know which documents they want to put through Mr. Jasarevic. Now, it's not oppressive for the Prosecutor to tell us that. They should tell us. We -- that's not prying into the secret councils of the Prosecutor. We need that information. It's axiomatic and I'm surprised that we meet now the comments that we do. When my learned friend says that there's been no changes of significance in the proofing notes. You only have to consider this witness and what he's told the Prosecutors at the last minute concerning his own part that he played. Whereas, the evidence is now in that for years he said nothing about that being right in on the death of Pero Maric and seeing a large number of extra bodies. You can see that the proofing notes are capable of revealing very significant new materials. It's also the fact that it's in proofing that we encounter in a strangely systematic way the allegations that the evil lawyer from Sefer Halilovic's team has been out there either threatening or bribing these witnesses. And so the proofing notes are of importance and should be given in a timely way. Of course, we recognise the realities that the Prosecutor has to live with and we understand that that may be that on occasion somebody will arrive late. But as Your Honour pointed out at the start and my friend didn't respond to, ten days is ten days. And in that case, we still didn't receive the notes. So I maintain the submission that I do. I make it clear I am not now asking for the trial to be delayed at all. I'm asking for it not to be delayed and that's why I'm asking the Prosecutors to hurry up. That's the submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just clarify this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- ten days. I believe one witness was here ten days because his testimony was put back. And proofing notes had been provided far before that. And the ten days was merely that he -- his testimony was put back. That's why he had to stay in The Hague. It's not that the proofing was done ten days later. It was done immediately and proofing notes were provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I just take that as an example because the witness himself, you know, told us that he had been here for ten days. But anyway, as a principle, I believe that it's the obligation of the Prosecution to furnish the proofing notes as well as the list of the documents to the Chamber as well as to the Defence as early as possible, as early as practical. That is a principle. And we will see, you know, whether there's any, you know, significant matters in the proofing notes. But generally speaking I don't think there are. But maybe in amount to occasions, there's some new elements in the proofing notes. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Just three very short matters. The first one relates to last week's discussion about the chain of custody of documents. We have reviewed the list of documents which for we requested to receive information pertaining to the chain of custody. And we've withdrawn two documents which could be considered as open-source documents, so we have withdrawn those ones and sent a fourth letter to the Prosecution about the chain of custody, and we would ask the Prosecution -- we have asked in that letter to the Prosecution to act expeditiously considering that some of those documents will be tendered very soon, as early as this week, through the two witnesses which have been mentioned earlier. Concerning the Rule 68 material, we've now received three translations from the Prosecution. We are very grateful for those documents. And we are also very keen to receive translation of the 11 other Rule 68 documents concerned by Your Honours' ruling. Finally, we would like to seek some clarification about the issue of the order of the 30th of August. Your Honour will remember that is the order which raised a number of issues in relation to the translation and the three different translations of the documents. And we would like to know whether Your Honour is expecting a motion in relation to this matter from the Defence or if the matter will be dealt with otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm so glad to hear that there are some translations of the documents, but still it is not enough. I believe that our trial is in process at this moment, so I hope that the Translation Section could put the materials in our case as a priority matter to deal -- to deal with. And, of course, as the August 30th decision, the Trial Chamber will make a decision on that issue because we have heard the both parties' positions on that issue, so there's no need to submit any papers. After all, we try to make it a non-paper trial in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The Defence counsel, Mr. Morrissey, is very kind to inform me that he will let you go back home today. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness D. Witness, yesterday I was asking you questions at the end of the day about the number of bodies that you had seen, and you'll recall I put to you a statement to a Mr. Mijokovic where you said you saw one body and I also put to you a statement that you made to the cantonal court where you described seeing one body. Now, I want to put to you a statement made to an ICTY investigator named Nikolai Mikhailov on the 27th -- or the 26th -- sorry, on the 25th and 27th of May in the year 2000 where the interviewer was Nikolai Mikhailov and the interpreter was Peter Hewitt. Do you remember giving an interview to Nikolai Mikhailov and the interpreter Peter Hewitt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember giving that statement, but the interpreter was not there most of the time. He might have spent some 15 minutes with us in all, because the investigator spoke Bosnian and he told me that the statement would immediately be on the file in the ICTY online because he was writing my statement into the laptop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it you didn't get the chance to inspect it and sign it. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read the statement, but I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, you signed every page of it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed every page, but I wasn't given the statement to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I had a conversation in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But it's the fact that although -- you don't read the English language, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the gentleman spoke Bosnian and he told me that the statement was both in Bosnian and English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course if the statement was in English, it was quite natural for them to translate it for me into Bosnian in order for me to be able to read it. However, nothing came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness -- I call for the original statement in that matter to be provided to the witness, and I want to ask him some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I request of the Prosecution that they provide the original copy of this statement as signed by the witness so that the witness can inspect it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, do you have it at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I have is a marked copy of my own. I understand that the Prosecutor would have it in court as the original of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a copy available but not the original. I'm not sure what the counsel really wants the original. Would a copy be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. I cut you off. Yes, I would be satisfied with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. If you would be kind enough to furnish that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: My copy is equally mark as counsel is, so I'm asking our case manager to see whether she can get one. If you can give us a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I indicate the witness not being an English speaker, I'm not concerned that the witness see any markings or writings upon it. I really want him to see the -- the signatures that are on it and in particular on the last page. So I'm in the Prosecutor's hands, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, mine has been more than just marked. I think it would be -- we're just sending case manager Ana to go and get a clean copy, Your Honour. And this will be 25th, 27th, 2000 statement just to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. Well, I'll ask some other questions while that's being done. I'm grateful to the Prosecutor in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). Could that be stricken, please. Witness D, didn't you have present in -- present with you at the time that this statement was completed an interpreter named Peter Hewitt?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours and Madam Prosecutor, I'm referring to page 7 of the -- of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right? There was an interpreter called Peter Hewitt present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions that I spent with Mr. Nikolai, the interpreter was present with us only for some 15 to 20 minutes when Nikolai required his presence, because he spoke Bosnian and thought that he was self-sufficient for a conversation in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at paragraph 2 here, Peter Hewitt appears to attest that he's been informed by a name - your name, Witness D - that you speak and understand the Bosnian language. Now, did you tell Peter Hewitt that you spoke and understand the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I speak Bosnian. That's my native tongue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Peter Hewitt appears to go on to attest this: "I have orally translated the above statement from the English language to the Bosnian language in the presence of" - your name, Witness D - "who appeared to have heard and understood my translation of this statement." Now, do you agree that Peter Hewitt did in fact read that -- that statement back to you in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't read it back to you in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't read it back to me in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we -- there was just Nikolai and myself there. I told you. The interpreter was there only for some 15 to 20 minutes and only when Nikolai required him to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at paragraph number -- whereabouts did this interview take place, by the way, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Marsal Tito Barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at paragraph 4, Mr. Hewitt appears to say this. He says you, he gives your name -- but he says: "[Witness D] has acknowledged the facts and the matters set out in his or her statement as translated by me are true to the best of his or her knowledge and recollection and has accordingly signed his or her signature where indicated." And then underneath it is a signature, Peter Hewitt, a date, 27 May 2000, and another signature underneath that, and that signature appears to be yours, Witness D. Now, first of all, didn't Mr. Hewitt read back this statement and get you to sign an acknowledgment that he had done so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I signed the statement in the presence of Mr. Nikolai and not the interpreter. Secondly, nobody read out my statement to me from English into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if that's Mr. Peter Hewitt's claim, you'd say that's a complete fabrication; nothing like that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did give a statement, but I did not hear it translated back from English into Bosnian, nor was the interpreter present throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, on page 5 of that -- of that statement, did you say this? And I'm going to read you a reasonably lengthy passage here. It's about 12 lines or so, Your Honours, and Madam Prosecutor, in the middle of the page. "After Sulejman Lujinovic had told me about what happened during the night, we left the house and walked along the village path towards the entrance to the village. When I left the house, I noticed traces of blood on the village road. We followed the traces of blood and on the ground between the river and the village path we found a dead body. There was a red building opposite the dead body, and on the other side of the path from where the dead body had been found. The body of this man was in civilian clothes. Although I did not approach the body, it looked like it was the body of a man of about 50 to 60 years old." Now, I'm going to stop there and ask you some questions about that passage. Firstly, is that true? Did Sulejman Lujinovic come and tell you some things after which you walked along the path to the entrance to the village and saw a dead body of a man 50 to 60 years old? Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that Sulejman Lujinovic came to me in the morning and told me that some people had been killed in the village during the night. For the rest, I saw this one civilian and this was immediately next to the road and to the house where people from the Independent Battalion slept and where I had slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was next to the Neretva, on the right bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And did you then go on to say this -- well, sorry, I -- did you say -- and what you've just explained there, that's what you told Mr. Mikhailov as well, isn't it, and hence it appears in the statement? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was saying that I saw the body, and that's true, that I did see the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So after telling Mr. Mikhailov that, you went on to say this - and again at page 5, it immediately follows what I've asked about - "Then we proceeded along the village path in the direction of the entrance to the village. We noticed another body lying on the ground between the riverbank and the village road. The distance between the first body and the second body was about 50 metres. The second body was wearing a camouflage -- sorry, a military camouflage uniform. In minute, the body was that of a man of about 35 to 40 years old. I did not know who the man in a military camouflage uniform was." Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about that passage. Firstly, is that true? Did you walk along the village path and notice a man in a military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness answers, perhaps I can indicate to counsel I have now the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. But I'll deal with that in a moment, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that true, that you walked along the village path and that you saw a man in a military camouflage uniform dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated that I saw a dead body in a camouflage uniform. I said that I saw five or six bodies along the Neretva River, and I don't remember the body in the camouflage uniform. I saw the other bodies, the five or six bodies. And as for the camouflage uniforms and as for soldiers, I never stated that they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you indicated before -- I read to you a passage about seeing one body, and you agreed that that was true and that you said that to Nikolai Mikhailov. Now, immediately following that -- the Nikolai Mikhailov statement, we have this detailed account of a man in military camouflage uniform. Now, I put it to you that that's in there because that's what you told Mr. Mikhailov. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that Mr. Mikhailov has simply invented this comment by you that you saw a second body wearing a military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we're talking here about certain other circumstances. Here I am not saying that he made things up. I'm only sure that I didn't say this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's not a question of one word though, is it, Mr. Witness D? Here you've indicated that there was a distance, a particular distance between the two bodies of 50 metres. You told him that, didn't you, that there was a 50-metre gap between the two bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say this. Camouflage uniforms, distances, I didn't look. I didn't measure the distances. There were bodies on the left -- on the right bank of the Neretva. There were bodies there. And as for 50 metres and that I continued walking with Sulejman and that there were men in camouflage uniforms, bodies, dead bodies in camouflage uniforms, all this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you see, you've already indicated that you didn't make contact with any senior officers about what you saw and you've indicated your explanations for that, but of course had you have seen a man in a military uniform, well, that would have been something that threatened your personal security; correct? In other words, somebody was killing soldiers so that would have threatened your personal security if you saw it; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had seen them and if soldiers had been killed, some of the commanders would have said that some of his men were missing because there were only BiH army soldiers there and I'm sure that the fact would have come known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except for one possibility, Witness D: If you already knew why he was dead and the fact that he was dead. And that's what I put to you is the truth; you did see this soldier and you didn't say anything about it because you knew how he came to be killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a soldier. I don't know how soldiers or a soldier got killed. I was never aware of the fact that any soldiers were killed in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this statement was read back to you and signed by you as being read back to you by Mr. Peter Hewitt, interpreter; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many times do I have to repeat that the statement was never read to me from English into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just once more after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown now the copy of that statement, please, and in particular I'd ask the assistance of the court staff, please, to collect from the Prosecutor the copy that they've kindly provided. And perhaps Court 7 could be displayed on the overhead projector, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this witness is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mentioned that there's some signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour is -- Your Honour is correct. I'm grateful for the -- for the continued assistance of the Chamber in that regard. Well, Your Honour, perhaps it isn't necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, one solution may be, if I could ask to go into the private session briefly for the purpose of showing this witness the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You see, there is another question arising out of the taking of this statement

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In proofing notes to -- rising from your meeting with the attorney Ms. Chana here, we have this sentence: "In respect of Nikolai, the investigate, the witness states that because Nikolai spoke the Bosnian language, Nikolai communicated with the witness directly and the interpreter would not take much part in the interview. The interpreter was typing on a laptop as he was talking. When the statement was finished, it was not read back to him and he signed notwithstanding." Now, does tell Ms. Chana that the interpreter was typing on the laptop as he was talking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When this gentleman, whatever his name is, when he was there for the 20 minutes or so, he was at the desk but he was not typing my statement. He had his own laptop and Nikolai had his laptop and he told me that this statement was being recorded online, via the Internet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell Ms. Chana that the interpreter was only used occasionally by Nikolai to -- to help with difficulties and was otherwise out of the room at all times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there for 20 minutes and then he came to Nikolai's assistance. From time to time, when Nikolai needed his assistance with some words, with some explanations of particular words, he would be called in to help. And I am repeating again: If you need me to repeat this 100 times, I will do that. He was not present all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Witness D, we're dealing here with the notes of an experienced and responsible Prosecutor. Are you seriously claiming that you told her that the interpreter was actually out of the room for most of the -- most of the interview? Are you claiming that you told her that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the interpreter wasn't there because Nikolai spoke Bosnian. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then let's be specific. You told, according to you, that -- you told Ms. Chana that the interpreter was out of the room for the majority of the taking of the statement; is that your claim or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I put it to you that that is a flat lie, that you did not tell the prosecuting counsel that at all. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. I said that Nikolai spoke Bosnian, that he did not need an interpreter, and I'm sure that I did precisely that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So do you agree with me anyway in this regard, that you didn't tell Dragan -- you didn't tell Mr. Mijokovic, you didn't tell Judge -- investigating judge Hadzic, and you didn't tell Nikolai Mikhailov about seeing any more bodies than just one - or in the case of Nikolai Mikhailov, two bodies? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. These statements were given under the coercion of the MUP. All these statements were given in the MUP. Whatever I didn't say to them, I have come to state here. And as far as this crime that happened in Grabovica, I've told you everything that I had to tell you. What else do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claimed that the statement to the cantonal court in Sarajevo with Judge Hadzic was done under coercion as well? Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give any statements to Judge Hadzic, only to Vladimir Spoljaric. I never met with Mr. Hadzic, and this is a lie if anybody says I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would the Court just excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll deal with that matter a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, I'm going to -- so -- and finally, you had an interview with Bernard Brun, an investigator, in June of 2004; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- did you admit to him that you'd seen more than one or two bodies? Did you admit to him that you'd seen your current number, five or six, or did you admit to him the number that you put to Ms. Chana, ten? Did you admit any of those things to Bernard Brun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what I said, but you can read a statement and you will see there. Whatever I said to Mr. Bernard is the fact, and I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I want to put to you is that you said to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I want to put to you is that you said to Mr. Bernard -- and this is at page 3, Your Honours, at paragraph 19 and 20 -- you told Bernard Brun that you'd been approached by a person, a phone call from Sefer Halilovic's lawyer and that the lawyer had asked you to make a material change to your statement in favour of his client, the change being to the effect "I did notice see Sefer Halilovic in Grabovica. I did not accept." And then at paragraph 20, did you go on to say this: "I explained it would be impossible for me to tell a different story to the one I have given several times to the ICTY investigator because -- as my statement is only reflecting the truth"? Did you say that to Bernard Brun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statement that I gave to Bernard Brun. And what Nikolai and MUP and the CSB wrote down the way they saw fit, this is a different story. As far as I am concerned, I was with Mr. Nikolai in Bembasa restaurant where I worked. Maybe this should be also mentioned. That was in 1998. Because I worked in that particular restaurant even before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Short, dark-haired, sporting a moustache. He was a Russian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. But what I'm putting to you is that when you spoke to Bernard Brun in June of 2004 - that's just last year - you didn't say anything about seeing five or six bodies or even ten bodies on that occasion, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of things they said or I didn't say, but I have stated them before this Tribunal. Somebody mentioned that I was sitting with Sefer's lawyer, Sefer or somebody offered me money, and until the very last moment Lutvo Mehonic and Azem Mehonic were telling me, "how much money do you need not to say what you said before?" Then I called Mr. Brun to ask him whether I could bring the money that they had given me as evidence. You're not asking me about my safety, about how I was threatened, how I was -- a knife was put at my throat and I was held at gunpoint. You're not asking me about that. You are asking me only about this man who approved all these crimes in Grabovica. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your policy to make that speech whenever you're getting caught out on one of your lies, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not making speeches. I'm just giving you the facts. And I'm not lying. I am telling you what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal with some facts, them -- then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would ask now that the -- because of the matter of signatures, I would ask to go back into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go back to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final question concerning the number of bodies is this: Did you come along to this Tribunal and tell the Prosecutor, Ms. Chana, that you'd seen ten bodies? Did you tell her that because you spoke to Mr. Mehanovic in the hotel room and he told you the Defence are going to catch you out on your story?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Ms. Chana that I saw up to ten bodies, up to ten bodies. And I never spoke to Nedzad Mehanovic about my statements or testimonies. Nedzad Mehanovic and I and all the other witnesses appearing here have their own testimonies. We have been long-time friends. We sat in a bar having a drink until midnight. And then we parted. We never discussed testimonies. Nedzad only told me to pay attention to counsel who may be provocative, who will put to me that I'm liar, and who will put some provocative questions to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must have been talking about the Prosecutors, Mr. -- Witness D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was a joke. I withdraw it. It was a joke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not about the Prosecutors. About Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Witness D, could I offer you my apologies. That was not said seriously, and you're entitled to be dealt with seriously, so I withdraw that question and apologise for making the comment. Could I move now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, Ms. Chana -- we have to hear her.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel, for their apology. Your Honour, I will take issue with something counsel has said earlier on, and when he says "did you tell Ms. Chana that you're going to be caught out --" I'm trying to find the -- that -- "Did you tell her that because you spoke to Mr. Mehanovic in the hotel room and he told you the Defence are going to catch you out on your story." Your Honour, there is a very strong innuendo there. I find that counsel has been doing this quite persistently. I have held my counsel up to now and I think it's important that counsel do not make such innuendos that I would have been told such a thing and it would not be reflected in the proofing notes. It does nothing but confuse the witness. If they are legitimate questions to be put to the witness, I entirely understand. Counsel does have an onerous burden in defending his client. But I think these are cheap attacks. Sorry, Your Honour, I have to say this. As I said, there are many times this has come up. And this time I have to take issue with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that Mr. Morrissey has already offered his apologies to the Prosecution, and I hope that, you know, in the -- in the future proceedings the -- in the direct examination or cross-examination the parties should make less mentioning of the other party unless there's hard evidence to show there's some irregularities on the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd seek to respond to both my friend's comments and those that Your Honour has just made. In the first place, there was no -- the initial thing that I said was an ill-timed joke at the end of a passage of cross-examination. It shouldn't have been made. That was what I apologised for, and it had nothing to do with any genuine attack. In fact, any analysis of it would make it quite clear that it was a -- it must have been obvious who Mr. Mehanovic was talking about, and I didn't take -- I didn't mean it and the witness didn't take it and I'm sure no one else in court would have taken that I was really attributing that to the Prosecutor. That was clearly a joke. Secondly, my learned friend indicated that he thought that the question contained an innuendo about the Prosecutor. Now, I want to be quite clear. It didn't. What Ms. Chana puts in the proofing notes, we are sure is accurate. In fact, quite the contrary to what Ms. Chana seems to be concerned about, what I'm putting is that it's the witness who is not now being frank about what he told to the Prosecutors. There is no attack on the Prosecutors. If the Prosecutors tell us that something was said in proofing, we are entitled to rely upon it and we do rely upon it, and we are entitled and we must be allowed to cross-examine upon it. There is no question here of Ms. Chana behaving improperly. To the contrary, we are relying on what she tells us as true. So I want to be clear that she should comfort herself from any thoughts that there's innuendo about her. What's being put is that what she told the Court as an officer of the court, and the Defence, is indeed what she was told. And we are entitled to have that. Ms. Chana has misconceived what the issue is. I'm putting here in asking those questions that the witness will change his ground whenever he feels the need to and will move away from things that he's said even to her even in recent times. Now, there is no valid objection to that line of cross-examination. We're given those notes for that exact purpose, and I have and I intend to continue to cross-examine this witness using that material and other materials that the Defence has provided to it. Secondly, I don't want the Prosecutor to make any more comments such as that it is an onerous task to defend Mr. Halilovic. On the contrary, it's pleasure to defend him. And if comments are to be made like that, let them be made in closing speeches, not in the middle of the case. Your Honours' comments that personal attacks should not happen are absolutely correct. I hope my words are interpreted at all times as not implying any attack on the Prosecutor unless I were to explicitly state that I was doing that. And I make it clear that I use these documents not for any purpose other than to deal with this witness, not with the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor is entitled to be shielded from cheap attacks, and I make it clear that the Tribunal is perfectly entitled to police that and ensure that the Defence do not do so. But I'm not doing that. We rely as truthful on what we're told in the proofing notes. Now, Your Honour, having thus unburdened myself, I hope that's of some comfort to the Prosecutor, because we're not impugning her integrity in the least. May I now continue with the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm grateful to counsel for that and I do understand and I think it's important that these issues be kept separate and I would just like to clarify one thing when I say counsel has an onerous burden, I did -- I think it has been misunderstood. What onerous burden means that I feel counsel has to do everything in his power for his client and I think counsel is doing a very good job in doing that. So I do understand that. I -- it was a misunderstanding on counsel's part when I said "what an onerous burden." It was not the way it was intended by me. But I am grateful for counsel's remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness D. I'll add my final apology to the list that I've just made. I apologise to you for the delay in questioning. Now I turn to your actions on the day following the killing of Pero Maric. Where were you at 9.00 the day following the killing of Pero Maric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th? You mean where I was on the 9th or on the 10th? Which -- which date are you referring to? The day after or that same day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the day following the killing of Pero Maric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my room, because I only just woke up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And, of course, your account is -- all right. And where were you at half past 9.00, half an hour later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had gone out of the house. With me was the gentleman who slept there in the same house, Erdin Arnautovic. Or actually, I -- I'm quite confused now. I can't remember -- I haven't really focussed on the question. I only know that I woke up at 9.00, and I must have been outside the house that I had slept in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it the fact that you hesitate about whether you were with Erdin Arnautovic because you suddenly remembered Arnautovic told you that he wasn't there that night. He was in Jablanica? Did you suddenly remember that your evidence might contradict Mr. Arnautovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Erdin Arnautovic at all. I only saw him as he was departing for Sarajevo. When I woke up, he was already packed up and he was waiting for the car to collect him and take him to the airport. Then as I came out of the elevator in the hotel, we only saw each other and greeted each other and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we're at cross-purposes, Witness D, and I'll take you back to the -- the 10th of -- of September. You've indicated you were in bed at 9.00 in the morning and then at 9.30 you were out of bed. Were you already walking around the village at 9.30?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I woke up, I went out and I saw this dead body between the house and -- I saw this trace of blood that went down the path towards the Neretva. Then I proceeded in the direction of the Neretva, where there were these five or six dead bodies lying next to the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you walk as far as the iron bridge or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you walk as far as the old railway station in which -- at the entrance to the village at which were located some of Solakovic's soldiers and indeed Solakovic himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any Solakovic soldiers that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Solakovic's soldiers were not billeted at the railway station, as you put it, but next to the house that I had slept in. That's the new -- newly built house that we could see on the photograph. And there was never a railway station there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never spoke to any of Solakovic's soldiers because I didn't know them and that's true for the entire independent group there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any of Solakovic's soldiers when you went out on this walk of yours at around 9.30 on the morning of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any -- did you see any refugees who had crossed over -- or sorry, did you see any refugees at all during that walk of yours at around 9.30 on the morning of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The refugees weren't there at all. They were on the other bank of the Neretva River in those cabins there and I never paid any attention to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the real truth this: There were a number of refugees over on your side of the village during the time of the killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in one house, where there were four or five of them; two children, a wife, and a husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P79. I'm sorry, Your Honour, it may be my mistake, but we don't have the one I asked for there on the screen. I'm asking for -- it's a photograph, and I believe -- it was a panoramic photograph. I believed it to be P79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness D, do you have in front of you now a photograph which has a number of small yellow numbers and small yellow arrows upon it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would ask some assistance from the court staff to assist the witness to put some marks upon this map -- on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On that map, would you please indicate -- well, first of all, on that map -- do you see on that map the small -- the white house with no roof that you say you were sleeping in in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you now draw with a dotted line the course of the walk that you took and stop the dotted line at the point where -- at the furthest point that you went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you please indicate -- yes. No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No objections? Yes, it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Defence Exhibit D189.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And after that walk, did you go and ask Nihad Vlahovljak what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting at that time when you were going for your walk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any masked men wandering the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that part of the walk, did you then walk up to the Pero Maric house, the scene of the killings the night before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to this house where this last arrow is. There's a friend called Regan there. I talked to him there and returned back to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please mark the house on that map -- I'm sorry, now -- that's been tendered into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown MFI189. And I'm going to get you to mark a couple of other things now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I ask the assistance of the court staff to help the witness to mark this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This MFI189 that you are about to be shown is the -- is the exhibit that you just marked a minute ago with the -- the course of your walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure the -- do I notice that there's a technical problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, there's a technical problem. Could you please ask this witness to re-mark it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- on this new photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I inquire: Did we lose the markings on the previous one? No. Very well. We would proceed again. If the witness could please be shown P79 again and we'll start from the start again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness D. Perhaps you'd just bear with us while we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we should have a break and during the break this issue could be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And just to make sure it's clear what's going to be done, I'll ask the witness to mark P79 with a couple extra locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. When we come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a break and then we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I was told that the technical problem has been fixed, so, Mr. Morrissey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness D. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown now P79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have in front of you once again that photograph with the yellow arrows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be given some assistance to draw on that again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could I just get you to mark just once again -- I'm sorry to do this to you, but because I neglected some other things, I want you to do it again. Could you mark with a dotted line once again the walk that you took at about 9.30 from your white house and along the -- the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you indicate, please, where you went after that with dotted lines. You've indicated that you went to see a friend called Regan, so can you indicate the course that you took to Regan's house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the house here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please place a number next to that house, number "1".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just put it --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You've marked it correctly. Is that the same house at which an individual named Turkovic, nicknamed Crni, was residing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crni did not reside in this house. He resided in this house over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the number 1 also the house where your friend Mr. Mehanovic was residing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehanovic? I saw him the first time only, and after that I didn't see him again. He was walking around. He didn't stay in one place only, and he was -- he stayed here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say -- could you mark Crni's house with a number "2", please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at which house do you say Mehanovic lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first night when we arrived, he was in this house, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark with a "3" which house he was in the first night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So just -- you've written that quite small. You're referring to Crni's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crni and Mehanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you mark with a "4" the house at which Mehanovic stayed after that, on the second night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I wouldn't know. I was not with Crni. I don't know where he stayed, where he slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I tender -- excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear about that, I'm asking about Mehanovic on that second night. Did you understand that was my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know. I don't know where he slept the second night. He was in the village, but I don't know where he slept on that second night. He was in the village though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I offer this document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No objections, I guess. So it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown photograph P177.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While this is being prepared, Witness D, I'm not going to ask you to mark this. I'm just going to show it to you and ask you to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I just -- oh, sorry, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you now have in front of you a photograph with two numbers marked on it inside red circles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the house on the right-hand side with number "1"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the other day -- in fact, on the 16th of February, Mr. Mehanovic marked this photograph. He indicated that that house number 1 was the one where he stayed. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you walk as far as that house on your morning walk or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no need for me to go there because none of us members slept in that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Mehanovic was your friend, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't he sleep in that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't sleep with him to know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time after you woke up at 9.00, 9.30, 10.00, 11.00, did you hear or see any shooting at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear or see any Croat civilians fleeing the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter didn't hear your answer on that occasion. Would you mind repeating it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any civilians crying out in fear of being raped or killed or robbed or otherwise mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Ramiz Delalic on that day, the day after the killings of Pero Maric and his wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, not on that day but the following day. Ramiz Delalic came with two children that he brought. I don't know where he found them. Maybe on the road to Jablanica as he was going towards Grabovica to see what happened -- what had happened. The crime had taken place in Grabovica and he came with two children. That was on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to come to that in just a moment. But as far as you're concerned and as far as you saw, all the killing was finished by the time you got out of bed at 9.30 in the morning the day after the Pero Maric murder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That following day, it's your account that -- let me just ask you some questions about the chronology so that I'm not confusing you in any way. Do you say that on the 10th of September, being the day after the Pero Maric killing, according to you, that the following things happened in order: Number one, you woke up and saw some bodies; number two, somewhere in the middle of the day Zuka arrived; and then number three, later in the day Ramiz arrived with the two children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not see some bodies. I saw five or six bodies along the Neretva --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we've -- we've been through that already and I'm just talking now about the -- about the timing of events. So is it -- is it your allegation that Zuka arrived in the village at about midday -- approximately midday, or do you say earlier or later than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon he came with his soldiers with lorries. He put up checkpoints. And I can show those checkpoints to you in the photo. He put up checkpoints in Grabovica. He said that nobody was to leave Grabovica without his approval, not a single soldier could leave Grabovica during that period of time without Zuka's arrival. He picked up the dead bodies. He loaded them onto the lorries and took them away. I don't know whether he loaded all the bodies, where he took them, in which direction. I don't know. I didn't hear and I was not abreast of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now answer my question: Approximately what time did Zuka arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. Maybe around noon. Maybe around 1.00. I can't be more precise than that. But in any case, it was before 3.00. I can't be more precise than that. I was -- I was not checking the time at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long do you say Zuka was there before he left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe half an hour. He picked up the victims --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And how long after Zuka left did Ramiz arrive with the boys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It -- it may have been 10, 15 minutes. They might have even crossed paths, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so how long was Ramiz in the village, approximately, with the children before he took them off to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes. He lined us up and the children recognised soldiers from our units. That's how long it took him to stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreter rendered your answer then as "the soldiers [sic] recognised some soldiers from your units." Is this an interpretation issue or do you say that the soldiers really did recognise -- the children really did recognise the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were supposed to identify us. We were lined up, and the children went from one soldier to another with Ramiz. Ramiz had a pistol in his hands and he was going to punish the person who had murdered his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you detailed questions about this in just a moment, but I'm just trying to get the chronology under control first. So after -- so Ramiz left, you would say, in the middle of the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in the afternoon. I don't know when exactly. I only know that he didn't stay long. He took the children, and he left for Jablanica, to the command there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And after that, you didn't see the children again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on that afternoon, coming towards evening, did Ramiz arrive back at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz returned within an hour. He returned to Grabovica. We were lined up. And in the evening at dusk we left off for Dreznica, which was to be our starting position for the first action that was supposed to take place in order to take the Antena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you -- approximately -- well, I'll ask you this: When you left for Dreznica, was it already dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dusk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have the shape of what you say happened on the 10th. I'm going to ask you some specific questions about Zuka and his involvement. Is it your claim that when Zuka came, he arrived in the village of Grabovica in person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zuka in person. I know him. I have known him since 1992 from Igman. He was the commander of that unit on Igman and then he withdrew to Jablanica once Igman fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what I put to you is that he arrived and he did indeed set up checkpoints at that point. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did set up checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I put to you is that you have made up the detail that Zuka took the bodies away. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not Zuka himself but his soldiers that collected the bodies, loaded them onto the lorries, and left together with Zuka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. But Zuka was -- according to you, Zuka was present right there while these villagers were loaded into trucks and taken away. Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zuka ask you, "Who did the killings"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not voice any comments. He did not ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Which one of the 9th Brigade left Grabovica prior to this and told Zuka what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I doubt that anybody went to tell the story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of whether or not Zuka was actually very fond of these villagers from Grabovica and had treated them very well in the preceding weeks? Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villages we are very fair and correct towards us, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. But did Zuka appear to you to be terribly unhappy and distraught at seeing the bodies of the dead Croat villagers, some of whom he knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not hear him comment or talk to any of the soldiers in Grabovica. Of all the troops, he didn't talk to anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't voice any comments about what happened, how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. This was my next series of questions for you. You're suggesting that Zuka came to the village and cleaned up the 9th Brigade's mess and didn't ask you any questions about what happened? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's just a lie by you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it's not a lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the body of the soldier, one of Zuka's own soldiers who you saw dead by the side of the road? Did he ask you any questions about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see the body of any dead soldiers by the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see the body of a soldier by the name of Kavlovic dead by the side of the road, a soldier of Zuka's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you tell Nikolai Mikhailov in that statement that we looked at earlier on that you'd seen a dead body of a soldier in military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I denied all of these statements. What I'm saying here is the truth. I'm giving this evidence under the oath. Whatever I said before, I'm denying everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not Zuka actually rescued some surviving Croat civilians from the village on the 9th of -- well, I won't ask you about a date. I'll just ask you first of all generally. Did you know that Zuka rescued some surviving Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Zuka saved any Croats. I only know that Ramiz Delalic saved the children, and that is a fact, and they are still the living witnesses of that. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) But let's just stay with Zuka for the moment now. I want to put a different proposition --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Prima facie I'm always wrong on these topics because of my criminal record, but I just haven't seen the line which my friend is referring to. I'm sorry. Could it just be specified which line it is and I might be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Line 22.11.21.42. That's the line. Yeah, 21.22 -- okay. Sorry, 22, 23, if you can read that, and 52, page 52. Page 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the page that my friend is referring to, is that page 52? Because that doesn't seem to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Line 22? Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm beginning to lose the line now. Yes, 22 to 23. It says: "Question," and it starts with: "Well, not only ..." It's going to the top of the page now. It's four lines down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Yes. Well, pardon me. Well, I agree with my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful to the Prosecutor for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, pardon me. I was about to put to you a different proposition about Zuka. I want to put to you that it's you and your friends who disposed of the bodies by burying them. Do you agree with that or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those people who were present at the killing of Pero Maric enlisted to do burying work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I did not hear any such order or command from anybody. I didn't hear anybody ordering anybody else to bury those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about telling those present at the killing of Pero Maric to help with killing the rest of the village? Were you in complete ignorance of that as well, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you blaming Zuka because you really do need someone to blame, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not blaming anybody. I'm just giving you the facts. Zuka came to pick up the dead civilians and take them away, and I don't know anything else. I'm not blaming Zuka for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown a clean copy of P79. Once again I'm going to ask the witness to have the opportunity to mark this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I take the opportunity of a little lull here? Can my submissions also be redacted before we go too far down the line, in respect of this matter that I raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a clean copy of that photograph in front of you now, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please mark with a "1" and a "2" the checkpoints set up by Zuka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints set up by the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please mark with a number "3" in a circle where you first saw the two boys with Ramiz.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the house where we were lined up, the house where I had slept. This is where we were lined up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of car -- sorry. I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I tender that -- that document. I offer it for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit D191.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of car did Ramiz arrive in when he brought the children?
