utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A jeep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of car did he depart in when he left with the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the colour of that jeep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he with a man from Zuka's unit with the nickname Spaga or Spago, who was a brown-haired man between 30 and 40 years old carrying a Heckler & Koch submachine-gun -- sorry, automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Spago, and I didn't pay any attention to the moment when Ramiz got out of the car with the two children. He was so angry that I really didn't pay attention to who else came with him. He only ordered us to line up in the meadow, and he said, "If any of the children recognise any of you, I will personally kill that person."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that line-up, was Dino Arnautovic included?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't claim that Dino Arnautovic is the one who drove Ramiz back to the village with the children and then subsequently drove him back to Jablanica again, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know actually who was there and who was missing. There was some 50 to 60 soldiers gathered up there, and these were really small children. I'm not really sure that they were able, as they were panic-stricken and afraid, to point out and identify who the killers were. And at that point I wasn't thinking about who was present and who was absent. I only know that the children went from one person to the other and failed to identify anyone. As for the presence of Dino Arnautovic, I cannot claim either way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, why is it that you said -- you suggested that Ramiz may have collected these children from the road to Jablanica? Was that based on something you were told or something that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Ramiz came to the village with these children, he said that he had found these small children distressed, weeping. He found them on a certain section of the M17 highway. They had told him that there was this crime in Grabovica that they had seen with their own eyes, their parents getting killed, and he said that he put them into his car and said, "I'm going to show you -- to identify the people who murdered them." And that's how things happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness D, just to be clear about the details of that, this is what Ramiz himself told you, isn't it? It's not something you've just made up? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there when he came with the children. There's nothing for me to really make up. Besides, these children are still alive and they can testify to the fact that Ramiz had saved them. Nobody else needs to corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just to be precise about it, the details of where it was that Ramiz found them were told to you by Ramiz himself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never told the story, not even now, as to where Ramiz had found the children, and I really don't know where he had found them, at which point of the road. If I knew, I would tell you that he found them at this and at this section of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. I understand that. But I'm just using your words. You mentioned the M17, and you mentioned that to this Tribunal for no other reason than Ramiz mentioned the M17 to you. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody mentioned the road to me. I know that the road is M17. That's where the road branches off in the direction of Grabovica, and this took place somewhere along the road and I know the name of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on page 57, at line 8 in your evidence a minute or so ago, you said this: "When Ramiz came to the village with these children, he said that he'd found these small children distressed and weeping." Now, that was the evidence you gave a minute ago and that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went on to say this: "He found them on a certain section of the M17 highway." And that's what you told the Tribunal a minute ago and that's what Ramiz told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the denomination of the road, and it was along that road that he had found them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you know that not because you were there watching him find them but because Ramiz told you that; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that because Ramiz had brought them over. Had it been someone else, I would have known it as well. Because Ramiz, as he arrived, very angry and nervous, he lined us up furiously in order for the children to identify the murderers. It was at that point that Ramiz saved the children and took them away to Jablanica. I don't know what happened to them eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just please try to focus on the precise question that you're being asked. You told this Tribunal that he found them on a certain section of the M17 highway; those are your words. And what I'm asking you is: Did Ramiz tell you that he'd found those children out on the highway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he told me so, that he had found them along the road from Jablanica to Grabovica. I didn't know anything about him finding them. I just know that he brought them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, please understand, I'm not accusing you of being present when he found these boys. And I understand what you say about where you were. But just to be perfectly clear about it, Ramiz was telling you that he found the boys on the Jablanica-to-Grabovica road not on that little side road which led into the right bank of the village; am I correct about that or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm -- I call that road M17. He said that he had found them along the Jablanica-Grabovica road, which is called M17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- I could tell you otherwise that it was on the Blagaj road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that it's M17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Am I right in understanding you in this way: Ramiz indicated that it was the highway but he didn't actually use the words "M17"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road from Jablanica to Grabovica, and I'm saying that that's M17. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all the same. He could have said that it was on the M17 or on the Jablanica-Grabovica road. The children were found and saved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. I understand your evidence on that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to put a proposition to this witness from another witness, and because of the matters raised by my learned friend before, I think we should go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see either of those children sleeping at Pero Maric's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen the children until Ramiz brought them over. I had never seen the two boys, underage boys. The first time I saw them was when Ramiz lined us up when they went from soldier to soldier to identify the killers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your house, the white house without a roof, was only about 50 metres away from Pero Maric's house, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be only -- far more than that. Not about 50, but at least 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's extend it to 100 metres then. It was a place where during your time in the village a base for your soldiers was established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood. What do you mean "set up, established"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, sorry, I'll take that back. It was a place where the -- it was a place where Ramiz went, quite frankly. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. What are you referring to? Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ramiz go to that house on the evening before the line-up took place to visit the two boys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I only know that I saw Ramiz Delalic the day he brought the children and I don't know anything else. I saw him that day. I saw him that day when he brought the children and went away with the children, and then I saw him when he came back and we set out for Dreznica. So these were the two occasions that I saw them on, on the 10th and -- now, I don't know if there were any other times that he came to the village. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And wasn't Pero Maric's house the place where stolen livestock was brought, stolen cows, calfs, goats, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this village was a very poor one, and I don't believe there was anything to steal there. There were just elderly people there. There was nothing to really be stolen. And you're claiming that we had a logistics centre there, and that's not true. As far as I know, nobody ever brought anything from Grabovica or took home with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were no calfs -- cows tied up outside Pero Maric's house waiting for you to eat them at a barbecue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we only slaughtered this one sheep or goat given to us by an old lady, and that was on the 8th. That's all I know. For the rest, we were receiving food from Zuka's base at Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the lady who gave you that -- that goat, where is she now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a Muslim refugee living together with a Croat family at this one house. Now, I didn't know them. We weren't relatives really in order for me to know which house they were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this lady who gave you the goat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: This lady was there before our arrival and after we left Grabovica heading for our operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this lady a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did she get a goat to give you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you ask the woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you'll have to forgive me, but I must ask you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know? I hadn't been living with them in the village in order to know where she got the goat from. You have to ask the woman where she got a goat or where -- whether she had a goat to give away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was her name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, whatever else may be said about Ramiz's present or absence in the village before this time, you deny that Ramiz came to the village the evening before this line-up took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was there. I didn't see him. Perhaps others may know more about it. I don't know who has information about it and who doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, after the line-up occurred, Ramiz took the boys in to Jablanica and he returned about an hour later, as you've indicated. Now, when Ramiz came back after the boys were safely in Jablanica, why didn't you - and I mean you, Witness D, not you the whole lot of you, but you personally - why didn't you go and approach him at that point and say, "I know who the shooters are"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we didn't have time at our hands in order to talk to people, because Ramiz arrived, the troops packed up, and then within the half hour set out for Dreznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that we had the orders from the Supreme Command headed by -- no, he remained there. I don't know where he went from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't actually get any written orders until you got an order from Zuka on the 11th of September headed "Operation defence of people's rights, Vrdi 93"? Isn't that accurate? A combat order signed by Zulfikar Alispago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who signed the order, but it wasn't on the 11th. It was on the 10th in the evening that we set out from Grabovica. It was at dusk. Whereas, on the 11th, the attack on the Antena took place. And on the 12th, the attack on Golubic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch the name of the other place --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- took place. And that was in the direction of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on what date -- well, I withdraw that. Very well. All right. Now, my last series of questions concerns the course of the investigation and so on from that day on until the present day. And then you are finished with cross-examination, Witness D. Now, it's the fact, isn't it, that on the -- that on the 26th of October you were questioned in the course of Operation Trebevic, a joint operation by military security forces and the civilian police, also known as the MUP, M-U-P; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the military security but, rather, the court, because nobody interviewed us from the military security body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you've indicated how you were treated by those people, but questions I've got now relate to the topic of the questions they pressed you about. Now, just listen carefully to what I put to you and tell me if it's accurate. Those questioners during the Trebevic operation questioned you about a number of different matters, not just Grabovica but also the supposed armed rebellion concerning members of the 9th Brigade and civilian police in July; is that accurate so far?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. They did interrogate us in relation to these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they also interrogated you about other alleged crimes, real or made up. Is that true too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I wasn't charged with any criminal offences, they didn't have any business questioning me about them. I don't know for the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that you had committed any criminal offences yourself, leaving aside, of course, Grabovica itself. What I'm putting to you is those interrogators were trying to get you to admit to things that you hadn't done. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were obviously trying to frame and set up Ramiz Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind. What sort of a set-up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. Perhaps the question wasn't a very good one. Did they ask you a lot of questions suggesting that they thought Ramiz had committed many different crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as many. Only a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. As far as you could see, the accusations that they were making were false, untrue accusations; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They did ask you a limited, small number of questions about Grabovica and the killings there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only once, and then the whole operation was drawn to a close by those in the authorities who were powerful enough to bring the proceedings to a stop because it was in their interest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just be clear about the questions that you were asked before we jump to the political side of this. You were questioned not just about Grabovica but about Sefer Halilovic and his role; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were questioning everyone, but it was all taking place under pressure, duress. We were being threatened with life imprisonment, regardless of whether we are guilty or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the kind of threats we were faced with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Look, and I better be clear with you. I'm not disputing with you that you were placed under severe and improper pressure at the time. But if you just deal with the question precisely. They did ask you questions at that time about Sefer Halilovic and his role in this operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were basically putting the same question to everyone. They were trying to have the case suit them. They would just put a question to you and ask you to answer in the affirmative or the negative without having any possibility to provide any additional explanations, because you were there treated as if you were the aggressor, the Chetnik. That's how they treated me in -- at the court and in the prison in Sarajevo. It was in the end Mr. Jusuf Jasarevic who released me and told me, "We deeply apologise. You were not to be blamed for anything and we hope that you would remain in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm afraid you did not answer the question put to you by Defence. The question is: They did ask you questions at that time about Sefer Halilovic and his role in this operation; correct? Answer yes or no -- it's a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just following on from that: At the time when they asked you those questions, it was obvious to you at that time that they were no friends of Sefer Halilovic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were his friends or not. I only know that Mr. Sefer Halilovic was removed from his position at the time and that he was placed under house arrest. I don't know what their position towards him was, but that's what the then-authorities decided upon. I don't know whether the command was involved. But I was never asked about my opinion of Sefer Halilovic. I thought that he was a good commander and that he was a good strategist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. Now, I want to put to you your words from the interrogation which took place on the 31st of October, 1993, while you were detained during Operation Trebevic. This is in the material provided to the Defence and to the Chamber by the Prosecutor, Your Honours, and it appears at the bottom of page 2. Did you tell the -- the police at that time this -- I'm going to read it to you so that you've got a clear picture of what you told the police and then you can comment upon that. "A month after these events, the assault detachment was again sent to Herzegovina front under the command of brigade commander Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo. We spent a total of seven days in Herzegovina. We operated on Antena Hill above the village of Vrdi and on Mount Medved." Now paragraph: "During the attack, the assault detachment was divided into two combat group, one of them attacking Mount Medved, the other, Antena Hill. Together with Nevzet Sabanovic, also known as Troka; Jasmin Medic, also known as Mede; Ertan Hukalic, Safet Koca, Nedzad Mehanovic, Amir Jusovic, Samed Memovic, Amel Cengic, Safet Dermaku, also known as Sok, Fadil Kurgac, Semsudin Herak, and Sulejman Lujinovic, also known as Lujo, I attacked Mount Medved. Together with us the men from the unit known as Cedo's Wolves took part in this attack. During operations on the Herzegovina front, the group I was in did not take part in attacks on any inhabited places. "Upon our return from Herzegovina to Sarajevo, Commander Ramiz Delalic rewarded me, Nevzet Sabanovic, Sulejman Lujinovic, Jasmin Medic, and Ertan Hukalic with pistols for courage shown. I received a Browning extended 9-millimetre 14-plus pistol, factory number 7654. "After we returned, we rested and carried on with our regular training." Now, firstly, have you understood what I read to you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. But Ramiz was not the commander in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not under his commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I understand that. But do you agree with this: Despite being asked about Sefer Halilovic's role, you said nothing at all about him being present or indeed Vehbija Karic being present at the time when the comment you allege about killing the Croat civilians was made? Do you agree there's not a reference, not a word about that in that section I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, this is the statement that I deny. They could have written whatever they wanted. But I am saying that Sefer Halilovic was the commander of the Neretva operation. He was the Chief of Staff. As for the rest, I don't know. The gentleman is here and he can tell you whether this is the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is this: You didn't tell those investigators at the time anything about Karic making the -- the comment about killing civilians and you didn't mention anything at all about Sefer Halilovic being nearby when this supposed comment was made, did you? Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree. This is what suited them. This was the policy. This is what they wrote. If they agreed with what you said, then they took your words as they were said. If they didn't like you, then they distorted your words. If they needed you, they did one thing. If they didn't need you, then they did another thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they have distorted my words. They wrote down whatever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. But you're not suggesting that they've hidden something negative you said about Sefer Halilovic, are you? You're not suggesting that they've covered up something negative to Sefer Halilovic, bearing in mind that he, too, was under house arrest and under investigation at that time, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all good and well, but they were looking after number one. Sefer also had somebody above him. He was not omnipotent. He had to talk to somebody about all these things. Maybe they -- these people were looking after themselves. The men at the top of the army knew a lot of what was going on. I don't know. I'm sure that things got covered up. There's a lot of that going -- still going on in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from that day that you were released from custody, you did not approach the authorities and tell them about the killings that you were close to or about the behaviour of Karic and Sefer Halilovic until the year 1998; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked that again. They started on the 26th of October, and this was not their goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a story being -- unfolded that suited nobody. And I said that and I said it yesterday. I've said it a number of times. I don't know what else to tell you. And once I left the central prison, I no longer wanted to be a member of that army because of the way I was treated and humiliated. I fared much worse off in that central prison than any aggressor would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just -- I understand what you say about that, but just stick with the questions for the moment. It was in 1998 that you first spoke to people in authority about what you say happened in the village of Grabovica; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1993, on the 26th of October - it was after that, maybe November, December - when I gave the first statement to Mr. Vladimir Spoljaric. And that was the only statement that I gave while I was in the central prison for four and a half months. The only statement I gave was that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the last thing you wanted to happen, the very last thing you wanted to happen, was for this series of murders in Grabovica to be properly investigated; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was powerless in that. It was -- it was war. And one life lost -- even to this very day in Sarajevo these things happen. I was just an ordinary person who couldn't do anything. And there were people above us, there were commanders, this commander, that commander, the commander of the army, the Chief of Staff, the president of the state, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to put to you that you and your colleagues who were present at the killings were very worried about Sefer Halilovic - and I'm going to list some reasons and then you can comment about it - you were worried about Halilovic because you knew he had given Namik Dzankovic the task of investigating this very crime on the night of the 9th of September. That's the first thing. I'm going to go through these in turn. And, secondly, you were worried about Sefer Halilovic because in 1995 he came out in the press demanding an inquiry into the Grabovica killings. And the third thing you were very worried about is that you knew that Sefer Halilovic had approached the ICTY himself in 1996 asking that these matters be looked at. So I put it to you on those bases, which you can comment on, that by 1996 you and the killers feared Sefer Halilovic and his campaign to have the truth come out. Now, do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to fear. I am not guilty of anything. And secondly, I know Sefer Halilovic very well. We have socialised. He came to my restaurant on several occasions. I asked him what was going on with regard to Grabovica. He said, "Nothing. Nothing will come of that." From 1964, the 1st of May, when I started working at Bembasa, I worked until 1997. Up to the month of March he was a guest there. And he never uttered any comments with -- with that regard. We were rather close. We were -- we greeted each other. We talked to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've asked you this question in other contexts, Witness D, but I'll have to ask it in this context too: Did you get round to telling the Prosecutor or the investigators or anyone else about these meetings and discussions with Mr. Halilovic in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not meetings. Those were not conversations. It was part of my work. He came to the restaurant where I worked. I was a waiter there. And that's when our contacts occurred. These were not meetings. We would just greet each other. Sometimes we would laugh, tell each other a joke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. But you knew about his campaign in the press, didn't you? You knew about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never read any such thing in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that he wrote a letter to Izetbegovic in 1995 asking that the matter be fully investigated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Presidency to know whether Izetbegovic received letters from Sefer Halilovic or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just a mortal being in Bosnia, a person who is trying to survive. I am not into politics. That's something I can't discuss. This is so far removed from -- from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you knew that Sefer Halilovic was pressing for an inquiry, did you and other members of the 9th Brigade take -- have a meeting in a restaurant called the Kiborg?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Counsel. I don't think he said that Halilovic was pressing for an inquiry. I think the witness has actually stated the opposite. The question was: Once you knew that Sefer Halilovic was pressing for an inquiry. Your Honour, the witness has categorically stated the opposite, that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, my friend's both wrong and right about that. So there's another problem with the question. I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 1996, did you have a meeting in a cafe called Kiborg with other members of the -- ex-members of the 9th Brigade to discuss how you were going to respond to the dangers of a potential investigation into Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can we go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, in 1998 did you make the statement that you've already been cross-examined on to an officer called Dragan Mijokovic on the 20th of March, 1998? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already commented upon these statements. What I'm saying here is the truth. And as for these statements, they were fabricated to suit somebody's needs, in the MUP, in the CSB, in the Bosnian courts. It was all a set-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement on the 20th of March, 1998, was that the first time you'd ever mentioned Sefer Halilovic's name in connection with the Karic threat or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I mentioned that, what had happened in Grabovica and that Sefer was the commander of the Neretva operation, was in the statement 1993, on the 26th onwards, during that period of time. I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then you went to the cantonal court on the 30th of the 11th, 1998 signing the record of the hearing of the witness, which has been tendered into evidence; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What statement? Of which witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the document I showed you earlier on with Judge Ibrahim Hadzic, clerk Edina Djurdjevic, which you said was a fabrication. Do you recall that document being shown on the projector?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it and I remember my signature. But this was never read to me. All these statements were written down the way it suited them. One thing would be added. One thing would be taken out. You have to understand that. The only truth is what I'm saying now as I sit here before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on the 25th and 27th of May of 2000, you spoke to Nikolai Mikhailov in the presence of the interpreter Peter Hewitt and produced a statement which you signed and had read back to you; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never read out to me. I've told you that already. And the interpreter wasn't there. You're asking me to confirm something that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on the 15th of June, 2004 you were interviewed by Bernard Brun.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, that document was read back to you in the same way that the previous one was; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bernard Brun was there and the interpreter was there and the interpreter read out the statement, unlike the previous time when Nikolai was there but the interpreter wasn't and the statement was not read out to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you point that out to Bernard Brun, say, "Gee, you do things differently to Nikolai"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in all that time you remained friendly and in contact with Ramiz Delalic? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. Ramiz was at large for five years. He was out of Sarajevo. He was not even in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and only for the last year he was in prison in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you say he was at large, what you mean is he was a fugitive from an incident that took place near the Saraj Hotel in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a fugitive but not because of that but because of a previous sentence that was -- he was supposed to serve six months in prison. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Pardon me. You're right about that, and I stand corrected. You recall there was an incident at the Saraj Hotel in 1997 in which the police wrongly accused Ramiz Delalic and you of joint offences against a man called Basovic? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the allegation was that you and Ramiz were jointly racketeering - it's a false allegation, but that was the allegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what -- what they claimed, but it was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I understand that, and you've never been convicted of that offence, have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never convicted. I didn't spend a single day in prison save for the time that I spent in prison from the 26th of October when I was arrested by the state. I did have a few misdemeanours, but I am an honest citizen, a law-abiding citizen, and I live with my family. We are all law-abiding citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, look, I'm not challenging you about misdemeanours, minor things, or anything of that nature. So set that at risk. I'm only asking you about the 1997 matter for one reason, and that is this: You were a close associate of Ramiz in 1997, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were friends, not associates. I don't know what you mean by "associates."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, as a general proposition, to conclude those statements, I want to put this to you: In all of those statements that you made, you minimised your involvement and in all of those statements that you made, you attacked Sefer Halilovic because -- well, perhaps I'll break it into two questions because it's unfair wrapped up into one. Do you agree that you minimised and significantly minimised your own involvement in all of those statements that I've just put to you? Do you agree with that or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't minimise anything. I was just a foot soldier. I didn't have any rank. I was not a commander. I was just a mere mortal. Whatever I said is exactly what happened. I am not attacking Sefer, Vehbija, or anybody else. I just told you the truth. And I'm not blaming anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, I put to you that you attacked Sefer Halilovic in those statements because he was a danger to you; in short you attacked him for the very reason that he was calling for an inquiry; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never called for any inquiry. Newspapers may have mentioned that, but if he had called for an inquiry, this would have been done, like any other inquiries that have taken place in Sarajevo ended up in convictions. If in 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999, 2000, anybody had raised that issue, all these people would have been convicted. What I am saying here is that nobody in the top echelons wanted this inquiry to take place. Sefer Halilovic was the minister in the government. He was in charge of refugees. He liked his position and it was not in his interest to -- to call for any inquiries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now, just wait a moment. The deal with this issue: Do you know a political party called the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- was that Alija Izetbegovic's party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic is dead; however, he was the founder of that party, rest in peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that also the party of Bakir Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I was never interested in that. I was never a member of any party. I was just not interested in that, so I wouldn't know what party he was a member of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was and remains the leader of an opposition political party to the SDA, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. It's a very small party. I don't know why -- why they would be like a big opposition. I don't know why the SDA would have anything to fear from that small party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether they've got anything to fear from that small party. I'm just asking you to confirm to the Tribunal that Sefer Halilovic is the leader of his own party to your certain knowledge. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the president of that party of his. I don't know what his position in the party is now, since he is here. In any case, he founded that party in 1994 or 1995. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that party was not part of the SDA. It was an opposition political party; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Really, I was not a member of any party. I just know the names, SDA, SDP, BPS, and so on and so forth. And I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But just --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they're opposition, whether they're a party in power, I don't know. I -- the only concern I have is how to survive. I couldn't care less about any party or people in power. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you say Sefer Halilovic was a minister in the government, he became a minister in the government after being elected at a democratic election standing for his own political party; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I'm sure that that was the case. If he hadn't been elected, he would not have been minister, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's right. But when you pointed -- made the point that he was a minister, you know very well, don't you, Mr. Witness D, that he's not a member of the SDA and he never has been a member of the SDA; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how things are. Parties come together. They -- they talk. Then when there are elections, when they are elected into parliament, they spend in parliament for three months, and then they all come together. There's one thing when they appear in public and another thing goes on when they're in private at the same table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But as you've indicated, you're a mortal man and you don't sit at that high table, do you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what you can go on -- just --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is no single mortal who can be put at the same table with them, who can find himself at the same table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I understand that. But just come back to the original question I asked you: You know that Sefer Halilovic was never a member of the SDA party, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Perhaps he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Okay. All right. The final questions concern this: On the 25th of January of this year, just a few weeks ago now, you were telephoned by Bernard Brun, the ICTY investigator; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the exact date, but I do know that he phoned me concerning my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Now, at that time, you claimed to him that you'd got 12 telephone calls on a mobile phone; isn't that right? You made that claim to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that I received his call -- that I received threatening calls.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, 12 of them on your mobile phone; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 10 or 12 calls that were placed on my mobile phone, but I could not trace them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you provide your telephone to the authorities for the purpose of them tracing back these telephones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's to no avail. Besides, I didn't have spare time to spend with the police and that sort of people. I knew that this would not come to anything anyway. Whenever something takes place in terms of a murder, a car bomb, in our country or any such threats --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please just stick to the question. Now, did you provide the telephone to the local police and, if not, did you provide the telephone to Bernard Brun so that he could pursue his inquiries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bernard Brun wasn't there. He was in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Otherwise. And that's when we spoke on the phone. I merely reported it to him, that there were such threats against me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't we do it now. Why don't you provide your phone now to The Hague authorities and then those numbers can be traced back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll provide you with my mobile right away. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Give it to the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are those numbers preserved still in that telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If weren't. How could they have been when the phone can only memorise up to ten calls and I had calls in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they've all gone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't memorise them. I didn't store them. Besides, the callers were hidden. You didn't have the caller ID on the phone when they called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you went on to tell Mr. Brun at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is -- this is at paragraph 12 of that affidavit, if the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're still willing to testify and you're not going to change your witness statement under any conditions. That's what you told Bernard Brun, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you were going to stick to your witness statement; correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was going to come to The Hague to testify, regardless of the threats and of what might happen to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. That's not the question. You said that "I am still willing to testify and I am not going to change my witness statement under any conditions." That's what you told Bernard Brun, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the phone, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You didn't tell him at that time -- just a minute.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be some sort of a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Look, let's wait. You didn't tell Bernard Brun at that time that you'd seen ten bodies -- at least ten bodies, and you didn't tell Bernard Brun at that time that you were right there when Pero Maric was shot, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't say that then, but I say it -- said it now before the Trial Chamber. Why would I tell them -- I was there in Nedzarici in the UN office and I was called by a lawyer and we met in the bar -- coffee-shop where they offered some money to me to change my testimony. So all the information was leaking. There was no security in place. Why should I risk my life? Would have place your life at risk right now? I mean, we're not children, are we?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to that 50.000 Deutschmarks, did you take that money? Did you accept the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could have been useful, couldn't it, to accept the money with the fingerprints of the bribing person upon it? Did you speak to the -- take investigators, the ICTY investigators about this and say, "Look, they're offering me a bribe"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did phone Mr. Bernard Brun and asked him whether I would -- should take the cash that they were offering me, these 50.000 German marks, and he told me that this was not advisable. I said, "But I could bring it over as evidence." But he dissuaded me from it, and that's what I stated here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In amongst all of the threats, bribes, and all the other things that have happened, have you ever actually been injured or have you ever actually received any money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't injured and I didn't take any money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if anyone wanted to shoot you, they had plenty of opportunities, didn't they, Witness D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. God knows what might happen upon my return to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But just -- no one knows what will happen in the future. But right now as things currently stand, you've been working in restaurant disclosure, I don't want to know the precise addresses of anywhere now. But you've been working in restaurants for many years and you've been easy to find, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that this would be no problem for them. Well, they are free to do what they wish to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Anyway, on the 28th of January, once again, Mr. Brun called you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I phoned Mr. Bernard Brun and then he phoned me the following day. That was actually in the evening, at 12.30 a.m. I phoned the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we have a -- an affidavit here - and I'm just going to give you your chance to say what you want to say about it - from Mr. Brun, who says: "On the 28th of January, 2005, at 16.15" -- this is at paragraph 13 F the Court pleases -- (redacted) (redacted) -- "I called [Witness D] once again with the aim to get the lawyer" -- the name -- I'm sorry, I'm being asked to slow down, Mr. Witness D, so just excuse me a moment, please. I'll read it again from the start: "On 28 January at 16.15, I called [Witness D] once again with the aim to get the name of the lawyer who offered him money at" -- a certain cafe, which is referred to in there. "Witness D said I could not get this information, but I have to explain that last night" -- something happened. You went on. And that's what he says about who made the phone call. Is it your claim that you made the phone call or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening on the 27th, I called him and Bernard Brun answered the phone. There was no interpreter. And since I don't speak any English, I merely introduced myself and rang off. That was my attempt to report this threat. And then the following day in the afternoon Mr. Bernard phoned -- or rather, through the interpreter - her name is Vesna, I believe - and then I told him the story as it happened that night in my entranceway of my apartment, where there were four masked people. One of them held me at gunpoint. The other held a knife at my throat. And they threatened that I had to change my testimony or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, we'll get to that frightening incident in just a moment. Right at the moment you're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, are you going to finish your cross-examination in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm going to finish this part of it in -- in two minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Not in five, but in -- in a period approximating half an hour and it could be less. And as usual, a break tends to make it go shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you know, we have been sitting here for one hour and 40 minutes. I think that's the extreme, you know, for -- for the tape, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Could I just say this: There's two minutes of this topic, but I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks, Witness D. Well, now, your claim -- you then -- so just finally: You say you rang Bernard Brun on the night of the 27th. And I want you to specify what time of night you called him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to believe me when I tell you that I don't know. I can't remember now. I'm all confused. When I returned from work, I believe that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And just finally, did you call him on your own mobile phone or -- or a home phone? I don't want to know the numbers, but which phone did you use to call him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you're able to provide that phone number to the Prosecutors if needs be; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Bernard Brun's mobile phone at home. I don't have it here with me. Here I have Ms. Vesna's number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you misunderstand. Your own telephone number, the number of your own mobile upon which phone you made this call on the 27th, you can give that number to the Prosecutors, can't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can give them my number. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the telephone records are going to reveal your telephone call to Bernard Brun at a certain time on the 27th; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, move on to what you said in this call. You told Bernard Brun that these men came and put a knife under your throat, and you did not mention in that telephone conversation anything to do with the gun, I suggest to you. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. I did mention it, but this must have been a misinterpretation. It was an error of interpretation. I did mention it to Bernard and to the gentleman from the security. I don't know what the name of the lady was, the one who came. I spent some 45 minutes with her in the car as we were moving around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask you about that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's the end of that part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey. Try to finish your cross in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aiming for about seven or eight. So we'll see what can be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Well, following the conversation with -- with Bernard Brun, you then spoke to members of the Witness -- Victims and Witnesses Unit and you told them on that occasion that you'd had a gun put to your head and didn't mention the knife; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told them what I told Mr. Bernard, that there was a knife at my throat and that there was a man holding a gun next to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and in due course you came to Hague and you arrived last Tuesday night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th at around 11.00 in the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you spent until about 12.30 that night drinking beer with your friend Mr. Mehanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also saw Dino Arnautovic that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer. The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said heard that night that Dino Arnautovic had just given evidence and it had gone pretty badly; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything of the sort. He only told me that Dino was there and that he went out into town. I never heard anything of -- about Dino's testimony. I only knew that he was to go home the day -- two days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was after the conversation with Mr. Mehanovic that for the very first time you revealed to attorney Chana that you were right there when Pero Maric was killed and that you'd seen ten bodies or more; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my conversation with Nedzad Mehanovic, we never discussed these matters, and I already told that to the lady during my proofing session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But just deal with my question. It was after the conversation with Mehanovic that for the first time ever you revealed to attorney Chana that you had in fact seen more than a couple of bodies; you'd seen ten bodies; and that you were right present when Pero Maric was brutally killed. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely told to Ms. Chana or to the Trial Chamber here. I've already said that on several occasions before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you'd never said it before you told Ms. Chana, had you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have occasion to and I would not feel safe enough. Who would provide me any guarantees if I were to say something like that in Sarajevo? I was exposed to threats anyhow. God knows how the situation might have gotten complicated had I really told so at that early stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a pardon from the government in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was pardoned in -- I was released in 1994, not in 1995. Jusuf Jasarevic came, who was chief of security of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or so I believe, and he came with release papers. I was released from the central prison in Sarajevo and it was on that occasion that he apologised to me, said that I was not to be blamed for anything, and that he hoped that I was going to continue my service for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that's exactly what you did do, because after being released from prison you came back and fought more. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join the 105th Brigade, as some other previous soldiers of the 9th Brigade did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't join any brigade. I was in the records of the 105th Brigade whilst I wasn't in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all from the 26th of October until the end of the war, until the Dayton Accords. So I wasn't a member of any brigade. I worked as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just to clarify your status there, please, is the situation this: That upon your release from prison, you were officially listed as being a member of the 105th Brigade but in fact you never did take up your position there? Is that an accurate way to capture the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witness D, you and I have parted company on a lot of matters here, but I just want to conclude by asking you about a couple of things. You actually spent a lot of that war being shot at by the aggressor and put in grave danger of a personal kind; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in combat activities. What does that mean that it poses a threat? There was danger in our everyday actions involving the aggressor. I was in the army and I can't say that I wasn't firing, shooting. I was on the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And farce -- as far as you were concerned, you were fighting to save the homes and the lives of your family and community from the ethnic cleansing and the atrocities that you thought might come from the aggressor; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was fighting for myself and my family. All those fighters who remained in this country, in this town, did so in order to protect their families, to prevent the Serb army, the aggressors, who had committed genocide against us, from entering the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you yourself never did favour the idea of ethnic cleansing against Bosnians of a Muslim or a Serbian or a Croatian background; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why should I be in favour of that? I never distinguished people according to their names. I never thought anything along those lines would have happened. I would not have been wounded in May 1992 had I thought so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whatever may have been the policies of the Republika Srpska and whatever may have been the policies of the HVO, as far as you were concerned, you knew of no policy of the Bosnian army or the Bosnian government to commit ethnic cleansing but, rather, you understood your army to be fighting for a multi-ethnic Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the town that I stayed in in Sarajevo, I don't know how many thousands of Serbs and Croats, people of other ethnicities, who continued living there, who were members of our units, Serbs and Croats. They were all there. And together we fought for this one and united Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D, thank you for your patience in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that's the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. But I have to say that you unintentionally [Realtime transcript read in error "intentionally"] disclosed the identity of this witness - that is not allowed - for several times, you know, during this proceedings. So in the future, I hope you could bear in mind my warning, and that kind of practice should not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do bear it in mind. Is Your Honour referring to something recent or just the general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The general comments from the very beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- of your cross-examination up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, could I just indicate one thing in relation to what Your Honour says. I did not intentionally disclose it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It just seemed to come out that way on the transcript. I acknowledge inadvertently doing it. We now have this document designed to warn me to say it. I do acknowledge that I did it, and I'm very sorry for doing it, and I'm happy to abide by any device or any assistance that anyone can give to keep me in line. And frankly, I do put it down to inexperience in this jurisdiction. I take it seriously, however, and we will endeavour to do much better in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Co-counsel is a very experienced person in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. I believe that in the future he will remind you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate he has a very heavy right foot and has been doing his best. It's not his fault, Your Honour; it's mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a few clarifications, if I may, Witness. Re-examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, counsel asked you a question and to which your response was that you had met Halilovic in 1997 at a cafe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the restaurant I worked for, and he was almost a daily guest in that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that - and I quote here - that "Nothing would come out of that." And this was in relation to any investigations in respect of Grabovica. I would like you to clarify. What was the nature of this conversation and why -- and what did you mean for him to understand when he said those words?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say, but in seeking clarification, I think that question itself needs clarification. My learned friend is entitled to ask if she wants to was there anything more to the conversation or was anything more said. But if you analyse the question asked there, it's got about five possible directions, and it far from clarifying, it, in my respectful submission, confuses. Now, I don't object to the witness being asked if he wants to, if he could remember anything further of the conversation that could be relevant, and my friend could legitimately ask it as arising out of cross-examination. That question there is apt to mislead, in my submission. So I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the witness answered in this way, so Ms. Chana is entitled to make some clarifications on that issue, and that's just what we want to hear. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Witness, let's go back to that conversation. Can you tell us what you recall of that conversation between you and Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came to the restaurant and sat down at the table, I would ask him about Grabovica, whether anything would come out of that, and then he said, "No, nothing will come out of that. This is forgotten, as it had -- it had -- had nothing happened."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said "whether anything would come out of that"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant was whether there -- there was an investigation being taken with regard to Grabovica. Because rumours started and newspapers started writing about this, and there were stories. The town was rife with stories about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he at that conversation tell you that he had in fact asked for an investigation in 1995, as it was put to you during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it -- it wasn't put to this witness at all that Sefer Halilovic told him any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. That's out of the scope.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm perhaps connecting two issues. Perhaps I'll take it one step at a time. It will become clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During cross-examination, counsel asked you whether you knew that Sefer Halilovic had asked for an investigation in 1995 in the papers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew of that, and I never heard that anybody had asked for such an investigation, and especially not Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were having this conversation in 1997 in the cafe, and you were saying "anything will come out of that," [sic] were you at that point ever asked -- told by Halilovic that he had in fact asked in 1995 for some investigations to be done into the matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. He never said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did he say, if anything, in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the other thing that you were asked about in cross-examination was about the murders of Pero Maric and his wife, and it is true that the first time you spoke about these murders was when you came to the proofing. Can you please now look into your own mind and tell the Court why is it that you came up with the Pero Maric murders and the fact that you were an eyewitness at the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I just felt the need to say that. For so many years that I knew it and the crime that had happened and nobody ever trying to elucidate those crimes, and all those who were there carry that memory in -- in them, and some -- some are more interested than others in knowing what -- what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your feelings about it, the murders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I -- I found it rather hard, all these civilians who were there, they were with us. They treated us as their children. They were with us all day. They welcomed us. They were not at all mean to us. And I -- I felt sorry for these people. And I carried them all this time on my mind, and I just couldn't -- could no longer bear with that. I felt that had to share that with somebody, somebody who would guarantee me that they would understand what had happened and that -- that they would sort of give me some guarantee of safety when I told them that this had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated to learned Defence counsel during his cross-examination that you did not go to the police, and I am not exactly quoting here. It's just a general purport of what was said. And I'm sure counsel will get onto his feet if it's not true -- that you didn't go to the police because essentially there was a cover-up. You used the word "cover-up." Could you please clarify to this Court, what do you mean by "a cover-up"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The state authorities covered everything up. People who were at the top did not want the whole thing to be clarified. They just wanted these perpetrators. They needed them. And as long as they needed them, they covered the whole thing up. The same went for Mr. Sefer Halilovic. For as long as they needed him, he was there. When they no longer needed him, they got rid of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that the reason you didn't go to the police, or was there any other reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been pointless for anybody to go to the police. I couldn't go to the police and report this crime in Grabovica because when I return home this was already something that anybody in my neighbourhood knew. My mother, for example, knew that this had happened. It had already been in the media. This genocide had already been reported. So even before I came home, actions could have been taken. My mother, for example, she knew, although she didn't have telephone, she didn't have many contacts with others. But this was brought by the media. Somebody who knew what had happened spread the word across the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all this time you did not say anything about this, because you have given several statements and I won't go into them, but they've been outlined by the learned Defence counsel as to the number of times you gave statements -- that you did not bring this issue up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, with respect, that's an objectionable question. That's not really what the witness has said. The witness has said that he -- those statements were either beaten out of him or bashed or that he didn't make them, in the case of cantonal court one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let me hear what the witness says this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. If the question could just be asked in a non-leading way, it's relevant and the materials are admissible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. Can you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have talked about the incidents in Grabovica at various times, from 1993 to now. This is not the first time you are ever talking about what happened in Grabovica. Is that not correct? But you have never mentioned the Maric murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to object, and it seems to be taking the witness's part here. I'm not sure if that really was his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I was going on from what he had previously said, that this is the first time he mentioned it, about the Pero Maric murders. He couldn't go to the police. And I was trying to invite him for further clarifications in that respect. I'm not allowed to lead the witness, Your Honour, so my hands are tied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other thing you -- you said to the Defence counsel during his cross-examination, that all the soldiers were aware of the murders. Can you clarify for us please. What do you mean by that, that all the soldiers were aware? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the soldiers were aware of the murders. They were all there. They were listening to what was going on, and they all commented upon that on their return to Sarajevo. Everybody knew exactly what had happened. The only thing is that they do not all remember the same thing and their versions differ somewhat. However, all the soldiers knew what had happened, irrespective of the fact who the perpetrators were. They were aware of the crime that had been committed in Grabovica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the soldiers were talking amongst themselves, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure that that arose out of -- out of cross-examination. This seems to be a new line of -- of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's at line 18:11:17:29 from the transcript, where this very question was raised by Defence counsel. I am very painfully aware that I must only ask questions which arose out of cross-examination. I've taken the trouble to even put the transcript line here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the soldiers were talking amongst each other about these murders in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
