utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they -- they did. And some even took pride at having seen what had happened, because some of them sought revenge for family members that they had lost, their mothers, fathers, brothers, and sisters. And yes, soldiers did talk about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these conversations or this -- any of the commanders ever present when this was happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, once again -- I mean, this is clearly material which if it was relevant to the case should have been led in evidence in chief. Now, it's never, never been put or cross-examined on that there was such a discussion in the presence of commanders, so that I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. That's a little bit, you know, over-extended.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I will not persist. But it is there. It was in the context of the Celo, the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Zigi [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know Zigi but I know Dzigi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dzigi. And you were asked by counsel was he at the -- was he there at the time of the Maric murders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met this person in Grabovica. They were Commander Divjak's men. And the only person I knew was Nihad Vlahovljak and Hajret. These were the only people I knew. And this person, Dzigi, I met only recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I want to take you to the part when you were talking about Celo bringing the youngsters and the line-up in relation do that -- to that. And the question was put to you by learned Defence counsel that Celo made a bona fide effort to find the killers. That was a question put to you and you responded. Now, what I would like to ask you is: Other than the killers pertaining to these two youngsters, did he make any other inquiries about any other killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this happened, these children came and he only inquired about the murders of the family of these two children, the father, the mother, and the little sister who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was not a general inquiry about the criminals.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then. He lined up all of us, and he asked the children to see if they could identify the murderers of -- of their parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next -- the next point I want to ask you about is when your brigade was asked to go to Herzegovina. And you had said in response to counsel's question that "Celo had no connection with us in Herzegovina." That was your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He did not have any command responsibility. We were placed under the command responsibility of Zulfikar Alispago, also known as Zuka. He was our commander there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- what percentage would you say of the 9th Brigade was sent to this operation in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you a -- a certain number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you give me the number of the -- the numbers of the brigade and how many went, the number of soldiers in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our brigade had about 5.000 troops, 5.000 fighters, including the logistics, the command, and everything else. And around 50 to 60 of us from the entire brigade went to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would make I want a very small percentage. I'm not a mathematician and I'm sure you're not either, but it would be fair to say it's a very small percentage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's about 1 per cent, 1.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the rest of the brigade doing who didn't go to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest remained in the town. They had their area of responsibility. I don't know how big that area was. In any case, they were manning positions and they were there in case of an attack. They remained defending the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if you know, Witness, that -- after the operation - I mean, after the 10th and when you came back to Sarajevo, wherever you went - do you know yourself any soldier that was missing, not in combat but from the situation in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that should really will clarified, if it's a reference to the killings or is it a reference to the line-up that took place subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm away from the line-up. I'm just generally saying that you -- you said that there were a number of units in Grabovica when you were there. Now, the question is this: Are you aware of anyone who went missing in Grabovica yourself? Are you aware of any soldier, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I now want to take you to the time Zuka comes to pick up these bodies. That was your evidence. Did you personally meet Zuka when he came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He parked his jeep in front of that house, and after him there were two lorries onto which the bodies were loaded, and there were two soldiers on each of the checkpoints that I had marked a while ago. They were involved in all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you meet him? Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zuka didn't talk to anybody. I know Zuka. I know Zuka well. He came with his soldiers. He placed two at each of the checkpoints. And the rest that had come in the lorries, they loaded the bodies onto those lorries and they drove off. I don't know in which direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Because, Witness, it was put to you by the counsel for the Defence that -- whether Zuka asked you any questions, and now you've responded that he did not speak to anyone and you did not speak to him either. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him speaking to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now to another point, Witness - and this will be my last point - you also indicated to the Defence -- it was a lengthy cross-examination about the whereabouts of Celo. It's in relation to that aspect of -- of the cross-examination. Would it have been possible for Celo to have come and gone from the village without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This would have not been possible. Somebody would have learnt of that. On that day when he brought the children and he -- when he lined us up and saved those children from certain death, this is the person who saved these children. I can say it here and I can say it and repeat again before as many people as -- as you wish. This -- he was the only person who saved these children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Witness, but I am not discussing about whether Celo saved the children or not. What I want to know is: You said somebody would have learnt about that. I'm asking about you yourself, wherever you were. Would it have been possible for Celo to have come and gone without you personally knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever Celo came, wherever we were, he would greet all the soldiers. He did not act as some big commander. We were all soldiers. And at -- on that day, I'm sure that he would have done the same if he had been there. I cannot deny that he was or that he wasn't. I can only tell you when I saw him, when he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana. Judge El Mahdi. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, this is a clarification I wish to have on a -- in the transcript yesterday, counsel for Defence asked you some questions concerning Mr. Delalic and his presence at Grabovica. Inter alia he asked you the following question. I quote what you say in English: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "for a short period of time did he come actually and join you in the village of Grabovica?" [Interpretation] And you answered, I quote you also in English. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "with the children. That was on the 9th at about 3.00 in the afternoon." End of quote. [Interpretation] A bit further, another question was asked from you: [In English]: "Did he ever take up a position in the white house that you accommodated yourself in?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "when we went into action, I don't know whether he spent that night there between the 9th and the 10th when he went into action." End of quotation. [Interpretation] My question is the following: Does your answer really reflect what you remember about this event? Is it exactly what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that the date is wrong. The children were brought on the 10th, not on the 9th. Ramiz brought them on the 10th and he stayed behind us in Grabovica. We went into our mission and he stayed in Grabovica together with some other men. I don't know who they were. And the rest of us went into our mission. I don't know if he slept there or not. When we returned, he waited for us in Jablanica. We got onto the lorries and went to Sarajevo. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Now you say that he came on the 10th with the children, on the 10th, not on the 9th, on the one hand; also, that he didn't spend the night from the 9th to the 10th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation] JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, he spent the night from the 10th to the 11th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed there on the 10th, yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Good. And is this a slip of the tongue or is it a problem with your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there may be a mistake in the -- in the date, a lapse in the date. I knew it was on the 10th, not on the 9th. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see none. At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that is that there may be. We would like to make a submission about it. It doesn't seem necessary to retain the witness nor to deal with the matter now. I would think it will take more than ten minutes to raise the matters I want to raise. But briefly they concern the effect of tendering statements. I bear in mind what Your Honour has already said about that, but there are certain matters I want to rely on arising out of those statements and I have a submission to make. What I thought the best way to deal with it, and it would be oppressive for the witness to be kept overnight, is to reserve the theoretical possibility of a videolink should there be a need to formally put documents. I can indicate there's certainly no more substantive cross-examination at all. But it's just a matter of whether these documents -- and I'm referring to statements here which we have from the Prosecutor -- whether or not those should be formally tendered and received into evidence. I don't want to simply say that they're not to be done now and lose my chance to do so later. If the Prosecution is content for this matter to be argued at a later time, I'm very content to do so and not retain the witness here. But that is a matter that I want to cover at some stage because I do have documents currently I wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Maybe we could find some other time to discuss this issue. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have indicated already to the Defence that we will be objecting to this, and since the witness is here be but this possibility of the videolink is a new -- a new one on me. And I would like to immediately answer to the extent that the witness has been here, counsel has had ample opportunity and unhindered by Your Honours' patience and the witness, and I think anything which needs to be raised should be done before the witness goes back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can indicate this in order to put it on the map. I seek to tender the -- all of the statements of this witness, and they can -- that can be debated at a later time. But I now seek while the witness is here to put that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we need some time to debate on that issue but not with the witness present, because those documents have been extensively used and shown to this witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I entirely agree with what Your Honour says. There are some matters of formality that arise as to the use that can properly be made about those statements. I've got submissions to be made about it. It's really a question for the -- I've indicated my position. Now, it's a question of whether the witness is permitted to go. In my submission, he should be permitted to go now. He's had a long day and has been here for quite a length of time. But if that's an obstacle to me putting the argument about tendering those documents, then I indicate I have got an argument to put about it. If the Prosecutor wants to maintain their position, well, that's their -- that's -- it's for them. But I have an argument to put about. I'm happy to put it now. I'm happy to do it tomorrow morning. It can be put in three weeks' time if that's what the Court wants as well. And that's why I raise, Your Honour, the issue of -- rather as we did with the witness Gusic -- the theoretical possibility that should there be some formal failing of -- failing to put a document - and I'm talk about the statements here, of course - to the witness, then that that could be accomplished in short by videolink without any histrionic cross-examination at a later time. But if my friend says that it all has to be done right now and if the Court be inclined to agree, well, then we can proceed now or we can proceed tomorrow morning. And the witness can remain. It's -- but I think it would be better to deal with it in the witness's absence, but -- and using the device that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that -- first, I don't think we need the witness here to solve this problem. Secondly, we don't see there's any advantage to have the videolink, you know, to connect with this witness because all those statements have been used very extensively during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we have the answers of this witness in the transcript. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I just make it clear that as indicated I'm proposing to rely on a number of matters arising out of those statements. And one of them is the -- the resemblance between the accounts given by this witness in -- in and around 1998 and the accounts given by his -- the other two witnesses at around the same time. Now, if the Prosecution wants to raise an objection at a later stage that these documents are not themselves in evidence, then I want them tendered because I want them to be in evidence to point to this very fact that we get this movement, almost like synchronised swimming at the Olympics, and I want to be able to point to that by pointing to evidence. If I can do it by reference to the material that's already before the Court, I don't need to tender it. But the Prosecution may say that those documents had to be tendered in order for me to make that argument. Now, they're not -- I understand that -- what Your Honour has indicated up to now is against that position, but I don't think the Prosecutor agrees with it. And that's why I'm not happily just conceding that it should happen, because I want to be in a position to rely on those matters when I come to make my arguments. And that's why I'm agonising now and raising the matter now rather than having to bring the witness back later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, the position of the Trial Chamber is very clear: Generally speaking as a normal practice we do not admit the previous statements into the evidence unless we have been persuaded by profound reasons there, we could reconsider our positions. But today it is not a good time to do that because it's already 2.00. We have been eating the time of our interpreters. They are very patient to allow us to sit 15 minutes more. So we will decide to send this witness back and we will discuss this matter at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will take you out of this room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the last word is that how about tomorrow's witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have two witnesses scheduled for tomorrow. If one is ill or -- or there is a problem, we'll just go with the other witness. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you could inform the Defence team as early as possible on whether that witness could be testifying tomorrow or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At the break, I suppose with the Victim and Witness Unit who was going over there to meet with him, and as soon as I receive some information, I'll let them know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the hearing for today is adjourned.
